This manuscript presents LCTfound, a diffusion-pretrained, cross-attention U-Net foundation model for lung CT trained on a very large multi-center dataset (LungCT-28M: 105,184 scans; “more than 28 million images” in the Abstract; “more than 20 million images” in Methods), and evaluated across eight tasks from clinical diagnosis/prognosis to pixel-level image enhancement. The breadth of downstream validations is notable: mediastinal neoplasm segmentation, PAP diagnosis, NSCLC prognostication and neoadjuvant MPR prediction, whole-lung 3D modeling for navigation, virtual CTA from non-contrast CT, sparse-view reconstruction, and low-dose CT enhancement. Across tasks, LCTfound generally outperforms strong pretraining baselines (e.g., MAE, MedSAM, RadImageNet), often with few-shot fine-tuning, with clear numeric gains reported (e.g., NSCLC AUC 0.704 on LUNG1 in Fig. 2; mediastinal neoplasm internal Dice 0.7895 in Fig. 3b; consistent improvements in pixel-level metrics in Fig. 5c-d and Supplementary Fig. 23). Pretraining with a DDPM and conditioning on basic clinical metadata (window width/level, etc.; “we employed a U-net architecture enhanced by the integration of transformer blocks,” Supplementary Fig. 1; “paired clinical information…after Bert encoding” in Curation of LungCT-28M and rationale of LCTfound) is technically sound and helps explain strong few-shot performance in both semantic and pixel-level tasks.

Several aspects strengthen the work. First, the scale and curation of LungCT-28M are impressive (“five medical centers across China,” 14 disease categories selected with an NLP classifier at confidence >0.9; Data cleaning of LungCT-28M). Second, the authors assess both high-level clinical endpoints (e.g., NSCLC survival, MPR) and low-level imaging tasks, showing that diffusion pretraining confers advantages for denoising/reconstruction (“pre-training eradicated the artifacts,” Fig. 5d; “cold diffusion” for low-dose enhancement, Supplementary Fig. 3b). Third, they provide ablations of linear vs full fine-tuning for prognosis (Fig. 2a–h), Grad-CAM visualizations (Supplementary Fig. 5, 10, 13) and deployment of full-lung 3D segmentation as a cloud demo (Fig. 4d and provided URL), underscoring translational potential.

At the same time, there are important issues that need to be addressed to solidify validity, transparency, and clinical credibility.

1) Human subjects ethics, data governance, and reporting standards
- The manuscript compiles multi-center, retrospective human imaging data, including minors (“age from 1 to 84 years,” Mediastinal neoplasms section) but does not state IRB/ethics committee approvals, consent/waiver, or data-sharing governance. Please add explicit ethics statements for each participating center, approval identifiers, consent procedures (including minors), and de-identification methods, in line with Nature Portfolio human research policies.
- For datasets involving rare diseases and multi-center cohorts (mediastinal neoplasms; MPR prediction), clarify data-use agreements and whether external test data remained on-site or were centrally transferred.

2) Dataset curation, leakage control, and generalizability
- Explicitly confirm that all downstream training/validation/test cohorts are patient-disjoint from the pretraining LungCT-28M and from each other, and that no site/time leakage occurs. This is particularly important where the pretraining NLP categories include diseases overlapping with downstream tasks (e.g., “Mediastinal mass (MM), 1,444 scans,” Fig. 1b).
- The counts for LungCT-28M images are inconsistent: Abstract says “more than 28 million images,” Methods state “more than 20 million images,” and Discussion mentions “over 100 million lung CT images” in the initial pool. Please reconcile and standardize these figures, and correct the stray term “ChestCT-100K” in the Discussion (line ~475), which is not defined elsewhere.
- For PAP diagnosis, specify that patients/sessions in training and testing are disjoint (“Guangzhou First People's Hospital,” PAP section) and clarify whether negatives in training/testing are from the same hospital/timeframe.
- Report scanner vendors, models, acquisition parameters, reconstruction kernels, and dose ranges for all datasets, and analyze domain shift (e.g., center/scanner/dose) and subgroup performance (e.g., sex/age) where feasible. The initial cohort provides sex composition (276,755 males and 209,130 females; Curation of LungCT-28M), but no disaggregated performance is reported.

3) Metrics, statistical rigor, and clinical evaluation
- Segmentation: The mediastinal neoplasm study reports Dice and external validation (Fig. 3b), but without confidence intervals or statistical tests. Please add CIs and significance testing across models, and lesion-level detection sensitivity if relevant. For whole-lung 3D modeling, reporting AUROC for segmentation is unusual; include standard overlap and boundary metrics (e.g., Dice/IoU, HD95, ASSD) across the 21 structures (Fig. 4b–d). Provide error bars and define them in figure legends.
- Classification/prognosis: For NSCLC survival on LUNG1 (Fig. 2), detail the thresholding strategy for KM stratification, provide hazard ratios with CIs from Cox models, and clarify whether multivariable analyses adjusted for known confounders (stage, histology, treatment). For MPR prediction, include CIs and calibration analyses; indicate how class imbalance was handled.
- Pixel-level tasks: For virtual CTA (Fig. 5c), the text appears internally inconsistent (“VIF…0.8600” as positive vs later “VIF…0.0831” labeled among negatively correlated metrics). Please correct the metric labels and ensure all metrics are defined in Methods. Augment quantitative image metrics with a radiologist reader study on vessel conspicuity, stenosis detection, or aneurysm/dissection depiction to establish clinical plausibility, and consider vessel segmentation overlap metrics.
- Sparse-view reconstruction uses only 9 training scans and a single test scan (561 images; Sparse view reconstruction section). Conclusions should be tempered; expand testing to multiple patients and report patient-level statistics. Clarify that CIs currently reflect slice-level variability, not subject-level generalization.
- Low-dose enhancement on Mayo 2016 uses 1 training and 9 test scans at “5% dose” (Methods). Beyond PSNR/SSIM/VIF/etc. (Supplementary Fig. 23), add HU fidelity analyses in ROIs (air, soft tissue, bone) and task-based assessments (e.g., nodule conspicuity or radiomics stability) to support clinical relevance.

4) Model design and ablations
- The architecture conditions on “paired clinical information” and time embeddings. Provide ablations quantifying the contribution of metadata conditioning (window width/level, disease tags) and multi-time-step features (“four different time steps,” Fine-tuning LCTfound) to downstream performance.
- Given the breadth of claims, include a consolidated comparison table summarizing improvements across all tasks to contextualize the stated “average 7.5% improvement” and “maximum 20% increase” (Introduction; Fig. 1d), and specify whether these are absolute or relative gains.
- Report inference time and computational footprint for downstream tasks, especially the clinically salient ones (full-lung 3D segmentation and mediastinal neoplasm segmentation), building on the limitation acknowledged about speed (Discussion).

5) Clarity, consistency, and reproducibility
- Ensure metric nomenclature is consistent (e.g., AUROC vs AUC), define all error bars in figure legends, and add missing definitions for segmentation metrics in Methods (currently focused on survival and pixel-level metrics).
- The mediastinal neoplasm section alternately refers to “four external medical centers” and “five external datasets” (Fig. 3a). Please reconcile this discrepancy and provide per-center counts (Supplementary Data Table 1 is referenced).
- Code availability is appreciated. Indicate whether pretrained weights and task-specific fine-tuned checkpoints will be released. For the NLP filtering pipeline used to curate LungCT-28M, provide model details and performance on held-out annotated reports.
- In Fig. 4, an access-token bearing URL is shared for the deployed demo. Please confirm that all content is de-identified and that sharing such tokens complies with institutional policies; consider removing static tokens from the paper.

6) Imaging and presentation standards
- In Methods, specify acquisition equipment and key settings for critical tasks (microscope-equivalent items here are scanner type, detector, reconstruction kernel, slice thickness, voxel size). Where images are displayed, clarify windowing, normalization, and any channel-wise adjustments, ensuring equal processing between methods in line with best practices outlined in community image standards.

Overall, the manuscript demonstrates a compelling advance: a single diffusion-pretrained foundation model that usefully spans high-level clinical tasks and low-level reconstruction/enhancement in lung CT. The multi-task breadth, few-shot competitiveness, and strong pixel-level performance are particularly noteworthy, as evidenced in Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 23. Addressing the ethical approvals, ensuring stricter statistical reporting and patient-level validation (notably for sparse-view reconstruction and low-dose enhancement), harmonizing dataset counts and metrics, and adding clinically grounded evaluations for virtual CTA and segmentation will substantially strengthen the paper’s rigor and translational impact.

My expertise covers medical imaging, machine learning for image analysis, and clinical AI evaluation; I did not independently verify the training code, and I did not assess the security/compliance of the provided web demo.

Only keep the least generic points.        8) You can incorporate Markdown and Latex into your review.        9) A total review has typically at least 300 and maximal 2000 words. Prefer your reviews to have between 500 and 1500 words.

[Standards for images]
Digital images submitted with a manuscript for review should be minimally processed.  A certain degree of image processing is acceptable for publication (and for some experiments, fields and techniques is unavoidable), but the final image must correctly represent the original data and conform to community standards. Editors may use software to screen images for manipulation.

Editors may request the unprocessed data files to help in manuscript evaluation during the peer review process; if these data are unavailable upon request, we may need to halt the peer review process until the issues are satisfactorily resolved.  We may also request unprocessed data when responding to post-publication issues that may arise with published papers. Lack of availability of unprocessed data can make resolution of post-publication issues challenging.  We recommend retaining unprocessed data and metadata files after publication, ideally archiving data in perpetuity.  

All life science papers published in Nature Portfolio journals require submission of unprocessed original images of gels and western blots to be submitted with the final accepted version. These unprocessed images are published in the Supplementary Information.

The guidelines below are intended to help in accurate presentation of image data.  Authors must also take care to avoid misrepresentation during data acquisition.  Please list all image acquisition tools and image processing software packages used and document key image-gathering settings and processing manipulations in the Methods.
- Images gathered at different times or from different locations should not be combined into a single image, unless it is stated that the resultant image is a product of time-averaged data or a time-lapse sequence. If juxtaposing images is essential, the borders should be clearly demarcated in the figure and described in the legend.
- The use of touch-up tools, such as cloning and healing tools in Photoshop, or any feature that deliberately obscures manipulations, is unacceptable.
- Processing (such as changing brightness and contrast) is appropriate only when it is applied equally across the entire image and is applied equally to controls. Contrast should not be adjusted so that data disappear. Excessive manipulations, such as processing to emphasize one region in the image at the expense of others (for example, through the use of a biased choice of threshold settings), is inappropriate, as is emphasizing experimental data relative to the control.



Electrophoretic gels and blots
- Quantitative comparisons between samples on different gels/blots are strongly discouraged; if this is unavoidable, the figure legend must state that the samples derive from the same experiment or parallel experiments and that gels/blots were processed in parallel. 
- Re-arranged lanes that are non-adjacent in the gel must be clearly indicated in a manner that delineates the boundary between the lanes. Re-arrangement of lanes should be stated as such in the figure legend. 
- Loading controls (e.g. GAPDH, actin) must be run on the same blot. When sample processing controls are run on different gels, they must be identified as such in the figure legend. Cropped gels in the paper must retain all important bands.
- High-contrast gels and blots are discouraged, as overexposure may mask additional bands.
- Authors should take care to check their manuscripts for the following (1) check figures for duplications (2) check blots and gels for splicing of lanes (3) indicate whether panels are sample processing or loading controls  (4) ensure that the unprocessed scans provided match the figures.



Microscopy
- Adjustments should be applied to the entire image. Threshold manipulation, expansion or contraction of signal ranges and the altering of high signals should be avoided. If "pseudo-colouring" and nonlinear adjustment (for example "gamma changes") are used, this must be disclosed. Adjustments of individual colour channels are sometimes necessary on "merged" images, but this should be noted in the figure legend.
- Cells from multiple fields should be grouped into a single field
We encourage inclusion of the following with the final revised version of the manuscript for publication: 
- In the Methods, specify the type of equipment (microscopes/objective lenses, cameras, detectors, filter model and batch number) and acquisition software used. Although we appreciate that there is some variation between instruments, equipment settings for critical measurements should also be listed.
- We encourage deposition of raw image files (including relevant metadata for example: acquisition information, including time and space resolution data (xyzt and pixel dimensions); image bit depth; experimental conditions such as temperature and imaging medium; and fluorochromes (excitation and emission wavelengths or ranges, filters, dichroic beamsplitters, if any)). 
- The display lookup table (LUT) and the quantitative map between the LUT and the bitmap should be provided, especially when rainbow pseudocolor is used. If the LUT is linear and covers the full range of the data, that should be stated.
- Processing software should be named in the methods section and any manipulations indicated in the relevant figure legends (such as type of deconvolution, three-dimensional reconstructions, surface and volume rendering, "gamma changes," filtering, thresholding and projection).
Authors should state the measured resolution at which an image was acquired and any downstream processing or averaging that enhances the resolution of the image.

[General research ethics]
Principles of scholarly freedom and scholarly responsibility
Researchers should be free to pursue lines of inquiry and the communication of knowledge and ideas without fear of repression or censorship. At the same time, they have the ethical obligation to uphold intellectual integrity and avoid preventable harms that may arise in the course of research or its communication.

Benefits and harms of research
Research should respect the dignity and rights of human research participants; of individuals or groups connected either with the research participants or the research topic; and of the communities in which research is carried out. Research should also respect the rights of non-human life, tangible and intangible heritage, natural resources, and the environment.

Harms can arise as a direct result of the conduct of research – for instance, injury to human participants in the course of participating in a research project; unnecessary suffering of non-human animals as a result of experimentation; material compromise of tangible heritage; ecosystem disruption etc. Harms can also arise indirectly, as a result of the publication of a research project or a piece of scholarly communication – for instance, stigmatization of a vulnerable human group or potential use of the results of research for unintended purposes (e.g., public policies that undermine human rights or misuse of information to threaten public health).

Non-maleficence and beneficence are two fundamental principles in research ethics requiring the maximization of benefits and minimization of potential harms. These principles form a core part of general frameworks for the ethical conduct of research across the sciences and humanities (for example, The World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki; The Belmont Report; the International Ethical Guidelines for Health-related Research Involving Humans; Ethics in Social Science and Humanities).

Advancing knowledge and understanding is a public good and, as such, a key benefit of research, even when the research in question does not have an obvious, immediate, or direct application. Although the pursuit of knowledge is a fundamental public good, considerations of harm can occasionally supersede the goal of seeking or sharing new knowledge, and a decision not to undertake or not to publish a project may be warranted. 

Consideration of risks and benefits (above and beyond any institutional ethics review) underlies the editorial process of all forms of scholarly communication in our publications. Editors consider harms that might result from the publication of a piece of scholarly communication, may seek external guidance on such potential risks of harm as part of the editorial process, and in cases of substantial risk of harm that outweighs any potential benefits, may decline publication (or correct, retract, remove or otherwise amend already published content).





Research involving animals or humans
All authors of life and social sciences manuscripts should ensure their compliance with the Nature Portfolio journals’ editorial policies.

Animal research
For primary research manuscripts in the Nature Portfolio journals reporting experiments on live vertebrates and/or higher invertebrates, the corresponding author must confirm that all experiments were performed in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. The manuscript must include a statement identifying the institutional and/or licensing committee approving the experiments, including any relevant details. Sex and other characteristics of animals that may influence results must be described. Details of housing and husbandry must be included where they are likely to influence experimental results. We recommend following the ARRIVE 2.0 reporting guidelines when documenting animal studies (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000411) We also recommend consulting the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals (2020), as a comprehensive resource for guidance on veterinary best practice for the euthanasia of animals. 
The Editor will take account of animal welfare issues and reserves the right to reject a manuscript, especially if the research involves protocols that are inconsistent with commonly accepted norms of animal research. Manuscripts presenting studies that have employed anesthesia or euthanasia methods inconsistent with the commonly accepted norms of veterinary best practice (e.g. chloral hydrate, ether, and chloroform) will not be considered. Decisions to not consider manuscripts presenting such anesthesia or euthanasia methods are independent of the approving ethics committee and any previously published work.

Research with human participants, their data or biological material

Human participants research

Race, ethnicity and racism
Race and ethnicity are sociopolitical constructs. Humans do not have biological races, at least based on modern biological criteria for the identification of geographical races or subspecies.

Studies that use the constructs of race and/or ethnicity should explicitly motivate their use. Race/ethnicity should not be used as proxies for other variables – for example, socioeconomic status or income. For studies involving data collected from human participants, researchers should explain:

- what the classification terms are;
- how racial/ethnic identity was determined (by the participants, the researchers or third parties).
This information should be provided in the Methods section of your manuscript and in the Reporting Summary.

Studies involving vulnerable groups

Criteria for publication
In general, to be acceptable, a paper should represent an advance in understanding likely to influence thinking in the field, with strong evidence for their conclusions. There should be a discernible reason why the work deserves the visibility of publication in a Nature Portfolio journal rather than the best of the specialist journals.

All submitted manuscripts are read by the editorial staff. To save time for authors and peer-reviewers, only those papers that seem most likely to meet our editorial criteria are sent for formal review. Those papers judged by the editors to be of insufficient general interest or otherwise inappropriate are rejected promptly without external review (although these decisions may be based on informal advice from specialists in the field).
Manuscripts judged to be of potential interest to our readership are sent for formal review, typically to two or three reviewers, but sometimes more if special advice is needed (for example on statistics or a particular technique). The editors then make a decision based on the reviewers' advice, from among several possibilities:
- Accept, with or without editorial revisions
- Invite the authors to revise their manuscript to address specific concerns before a final decision is reached
- Reject, but indicate to the authors that further work might justify a resubmission
- Reject outright, typically on grounds of specialist interest, lack of novelty, insufficient conceptual advance or major technical and/or interpretational problems

Setting out the arguments for and against publication is often more helpful to the editors than a direct recommendation one way or the other.
Editorial decisions are not a matter of counting votes or numerical rank assessments, and we do not always follow the majority recommendation. We try to evaluate the strength of the arguments raised by each reviewer and by the authors, and we may also consider other information not available to either party. - Key results: Please summarise what you consider to be the outstanding features of the work.
- Validity: Does the manuscript have flaws which should prohibit its publication? If so, please provide details.
- Originality and significance: If the conclusions are not original, please provide relevant references. On a more subjective note, do you feel that the results presented are of immediate interest to many people in your own discipline, and/or to people from several disciplines?
- Data & methodology: Please comment on the validity of the approach, quality of the data and quality of presentation. Please note that we expect our reviewers to review all data, including any extended data and supplementary information. Is the reporting of data and methodology sufficiently detailed and transparent to enable reproducing the results?
- Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties: All error bars should be defined in the corresponding figure legends; please comment if that’s not the case. Please include in your report a specific comment on the appropriateness of any statistical tests, and the accuracy of the description of any error bars and probability values.
- Conclusions: Do you find that the conclusions and data interpretation are robust, valid and reliable?
- Suggested improvements: Please list additional experiments or data that could help strengthening the work in a revision.
- References: Does this manuscript reference previous literature appropriately? If not, what references should be included or excluded?
- Clarity and context: Is the abstract clear, accessible? Are abstract, introduction and conclusions appropriate?
- Inflammatory material: Does the manuscript contain any language that is inappropriate or potentially libelous?
Springer Nature is committed to diversity, equity and inclusion; please raise any concerns that may in your view have an impact on this commitment.
Please indicate any particular part of the manuscript, data, or analyses that you feel is outside the scope of your expertise, or that you were unable to assess fully.

Reports do not necessarily need to follow this specific order but should document the referees' thought process. All statements should be justified and argued in detail, naming facts and citing supporting references, commenting on all aspects that are relevant to the manuscript and that the referees feel qualified commenting on. Principles of scholarly freedom and scholarly responsibility
Researchers should be free to pursue lines of inquiry and the communication of knowledge and ideas without fear of repression or censorship. At the same time, they have the ethical obligation to uphold intellectual integrity and avoid preventable harms that may arise in the course of research or its communication.

Benefits and harms of research

- what the classification terms are;
- how racial/ethnic identity was determined (by the participants, the researchers or third parties).

Gender – refers to socially constructed and enacted roles and behaviours which occur in a historical and cultural context and vary across societies and over time. Gender is usually incorrectly conceptualized as a binary (man / woman or feminine/masculine) factor. In reality, there is a spectrum of gender identities and expressions defining how individuals identify themselves and express their gender 
Gender identity – an individual’s conception of self as being a man, woman, masculine, feminine, nonbinary, ambivalent, etc., based in part on physical, psychological and social factors. It is the internal experience of a gender role. There is a broad range of gender identities including, but not limited to, transgender, gender-queer, gender-fluid, non-binary, gender-variant, genderless, agender, nongender, bi-gender, trans man, trans woman, trans masculine, trans feminine and cisgender 
Gender presentation – how a person publicly expresses or presents their gender identity. This can include behaviour and outward appearance such as dress, hair, make-up, body language and voice. A person’s chosen name and pronouns are also common ways of expressing gender. Others perceive a person’s gender through these attributes. Another term is “gender expression.”
"Gender" refers to a set of cultural norms and expectations and not a “biologically defined variable”. Such norms are not fixed but evolve across time and space. As such, definitions will require frequent revisiting, as the exercise of defining gender (and sexuality) is under constant flux and evolution, as is the area of study in itself.

# Abstract
The concomitant development and evolution of lung computed tomography (CT) and 26 artificial intelligence (AI) has allowed non-invasive lung imaging to be a key part of the 27 clinical care of patients with major diseases, such as lung cancer. However, the paucity 28 of labeled lung CT data has limited the training highly efficacious AI models and thereby 29 has retarded broad-scale adoption and deployment of AI-based lung CT imaging in the 30 real-world clinical setting. In this paper, We introduce LCTfound, a foundational model 31 that encodes images along with correlated clinical information, into a neural network. 32 LCTfound used self-supervised learning pre-trained by diffusion models using a large 33 dataset containing 105,184 lung CT scans (totaling more than 28 million images) from 34 multiple centers. LCTfound was evaluated on 8 categories of lung CT tasks, ranging from 35 scanning-level clinical diagnosis to pixel-level image restoration, including segmentation 36 of mediastinal neoplasm, diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, prognosis of non37 small  cell  lung  cancer,  prediction  of  major  pathological  response  to  neoadjuvant 38 chemoimmunotherapy,  whole  lung  3D  modeling  for  surgical  navigation,  virtual  lung 39 computed tomography angiography(CTA), reconstruction of lung CT from sparse views, 40 and enhancement of low-dose CT images. Equipped with the robust few-shot learning 41 capability, LCTfound outperformed the previously state-of-the-art pre-trained models in 42 all the above tasks. LCTfound is a major advancements in self-supervised representation 43 learning on lung CT, laying the groundwork for a foundational model that operates with 44 high efficacy across the spectrum of low-level and high-level clinical tasks and serving a 45 dual purpose in aiding in clinical diagnosis of lung diseases and improving the quality of 46 lung CT imaging. 47

48

# Introduction 49
- As an integral part of clinical imaging, the lung computed tomography (CT) is crucial for 50 doctors to examine the structure and function of key anatomical regions within the chest, 51 including the heart, lungs, related system organs including blood vessels and the spine 152 5 .  Annually,  hundreds  of  millions  of  lung  CT  are  performed  globally  as  lung  CT  is 53 indispensable  for  a  multitude  of  clinical  tasks,  ranging  from  disease  detection 6 and 54 continuous monitoring of disease states, to diagnostic evaluation of common and rare 55 lung  condition  to  preoperative  strategic  planning.  Concurrently,  the  development, 56 evolution and application of medical AI systems for lung CT has substantially eased the 57 workload in areas such as surgical navigation for lung operations, staging of lung cancer 7 , 58 and prognosis for lung cancer 8,9 , while also augmenting the imaging capabilities of lung 59
- CT systems. 60
- However, the creation of newer and more sophisticated medical AI systems typically 61 relies on massive amounts and meticulously curated datasets that require laborious and 62 time-intensive labeling that are tailored for specific clinical downstream tasks. The lack 63 of doctors with domain knowledge in lung CT and the prolonged process of gathering 64 sufficient data render the compilation of large, annotated datasets for individual lung CT 65 scans and related medical tasks costly and challenging 10-12 . This is particularly true for 66 rare  lung  diseases,  where  obtaining  enough  clinical  cases  to  train  comprehensive  AI 67 models is often impractical, leading to limitations in the performance of the currently 68 trained AI lung CT models. 69
- With  a  breakthroughs  in  large  language  and  vision  models  like  ChatGPT 13-15 , 70 CLIP 16 ,  SimCLR 17 ,  and DINO 18 ,  medical foundation models are now providing novel 71 solutions  to  address  theses  chanllenges.  Foundation  models  have  been  developed  in 72 computational pathology 1 , ophthalmic disease diagnosis 20,21 , ultrasonography, and cancer 73 biomarker innovation 22 , improving diagnostic accuracy, facilitating knowledge sharing 23 , 74

and  furthering  medical  education.  Foundational  models  that  are  trained  via  self75 supervised  learning  (SSL)  on  extremely  large  datasets  without  labelling.  Foundation 76 models are proficient at learning knowledge representations with ability for zero-shot or 77 few-shot learning, enabling these models to be fine-tuned for a multitude of downstream 78 applications 24 . 79

Foundation models for lung CT have not yet been developed, despite the board 80 applications of AI in the field of lung CT. For example, AI integrates the outcomes of 81 lung CT examination with clinical symptoms, exposure history, and laboratory tests to 82 quickly diagnose COVID-19 in patients 8,25,26 .  Three-dimensional deep learning neural 83 networks,  leveraging  low-dose  lung  CT  imaging,  enable  lung  cancer  screening,  with 84 diagnostic accuracy that exceeds radiologists 7 . A modularized neural network has been 85 engineered for reconstructing low-dose lung CT images, achieving a reconstruction speed 86 that greatly outpaces commercialized iterative approaches, while maintaining the quality 87 of the reconstruction 27 . Thus, foundation models in lung CT imaging can be expected to 88 serve  a  dual  purpose:  offering  clinical  insights  to  provide  diagnostic  and  therapeutic 89 support  and  enhancing  the  imaging  technology  of  CT  scanners  to  improve  practical 90 operations. 91

In  this  study,  we  present  LCTfound,  a  lung  CT  foundational  model  integrating 92 images with correlated fundamental clinical infomation into the neural network, which is 93 pre-trained by the diffusion policy on LungCT-28M (Fig. 1a) to address the dual purpose 94 role of lung CT. We used the LungCT-28M dataset is an extensive collection tailored for 95 lung CT, incorporating 105,184 lung CT scans from 5 centers, comprising over 28 million 96 images that encompass 14 distinct diseases(Fig. 1b). To our knowledge, this represents 97 the largest lung CT dataset to date, covering the widest range of comprehensive disease 98 states. By capitalizing on the LungCT-28M, we developed a feature encoder and decoder 99 employing SSL through a denoising diffusion probabilistic model 28 (DDPM, Fig. 1c), 100

which is adept at few-shot generalization across multiple downstream tasks leveraging 101 the extracted features. We validated the clinical and technical significance of LCTfound 102 across scaning-level to pixel-level downstream tasks. These tasks include the diagnosis 103 of low-incidence diseases (e.g., mediastinal neoplasm and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis 104 (PAP)), the prognosis prediction of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLS), the prediction 105 of major pathological response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, three-dimensional 106 whole lung modelingvirtual lung CTA imaging, the reconstruction of sparse views lung 107 CT and the enhancement of low dose lung CT (Fig. 1d). When benchmarked against 108 conventional vision pre-trained models such as like MAE 29 and MedSAM 30 in these tasks, 109 LCTfound  consistently outperformed these counterparts (with an average  7.5% 110 improvement  over  the  second-ranked  models,  and  a  maximum  20%  increase  in 111 performance over existing models). 112
# Results 113

# Curation of LungCT-28M and rationale of LCTfound 114
We  assembled  a  large  national  lung  CT  dataset,  with  485,885  scans,  from  patients 115 enrolled between 2009 and 2023 over 15 years (276,755 males and 209,130 females,) 116 from five medical centers across China (Fig. 1a). We refined this dataset based on the 117 quality  of  images  and  the  completeness  of  diagnostic  information  provided  in  the 118 accompanying medical reports. This process culminated in the creation of the pre-training 119 dataset,  LungCT-28M (Fig. 1a, Methods), which encompasses 105,184 scans (59,935 120 from males and 45,249 from females). Excluding the cohort of 14,756 Lung CT scans 121 with  no  evidence  of  disease,  the  final  LungCT-28M  dataset  for  training  the  model 122 comprised  CT  scans  for  14  common  lung  diseases,  with  the  following  distribution: 123 Diffuse parenchymal lung diseases (DPLD, 49,133 scans), pulmonary calcification (PC, 124 36,379 scans), Pulmonary bullae (PB, 19,029 scans), Lymph node enlargement (LNE, 125 16,967  scans),  Pulmonary  fibrosis  (PF,  16,945  scans),  bronchiectasis  (BCH,  16,302 126 scans),  Emphysema  (13,961  scans),  Pleural  effusion  (PE,  12,326  scans),  Pulmonary 127

cavity (PC, 5,544 scans), atelectasis (5,169 scans), Pneumothorax (PTX, 2,798 scans), 128 Tracheal  mass  (TM,  1,535  scans),  Mediastinal  mass  (MM,  1,444  scans),  and  Rib 129 Fractures (RF, 649 scans) (Fig. 1b). The primary scanning protocol of LungCT-28M is 130 chiefly  guided by clinical application requirements, specifically choosing the window 131 width and window level. 132

During  the  training  phase,  we  employed  a  U-net  architecture  enhanced  by  the 133 integration of transformer blocks 31 , encompassing roughly 200M trainable 134 parameters(Supplementary Fig. 1). Paired clinical information (such as window width, 135 window level,  etc.)  was  randomly  selected  and  after  Bert  encoding,  coupled  with  its 136 corresponding lung CT images, inputed into the main backbone network of LCTfound. 137 The  self-supervised  pre-training  LCTfound  is  grounded  in  the  core  principles  of 138 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM): A two-dimensional lung CT image 139 and its  basic  information  were  randomly  selected  from  the  LungCT-28M  dataset  and 140 subjected to data augmentation. During the forward propagation, we progressively added 141 Gaussian noise with a specific intensity into the image. After 1000 steps, this process 142 resulted in the transformation of the image into pure noise (Fig. 1c). During the backward 143 propagation, the neural network  learnt to perform denoising, thereby acquiring 144 representation learning abilities(Methods). The basic information of the lung CT images 145 was  used  as  guidance,  being  input  into  the  model  simultaneously.  To  strengthen  the 146 robustness  of  the  main  backbone  network  to  these  basic  information,  we  randomly 147 occluded part or all of the basic information as input. For the inference stage, the pre148 trained LCTfound was employed as a potent image encoder-decoder. For localization of 149 mediastinal neoplasms and whole lung segmentation, we applyed a trainable multilayer 150 perceptron  (MLP)  during  fine-tuning  process.  This  MLP  served  as  a  fusion  layer  for 151 features  integrating  from  the  decoding  path  to  obtain  the  final  segmentation  mask 152 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). For tasks like PAP diagnosis and NSCLC prognosis prediction, 153 we employ a trainable MLP to transform the bottom output features of the encoder to 154

- diagnostic labels(Supplementary Fig. 2b). For pixel-level tasks such as sparse-view lung 155 CT reconstruction, LCTfound was used as a feature dictionary to guide the restoration of 156 low-quality lung CT images(Supplementary Fig. 3a). For low-dose lung CT 157 enhancement, LCTfound was fine-tuned on downsteam task data through cold-diffusion 158 manner 32 (Supplementary Fig. 3b). 159

# LCTfound improves NSCLC prognostication and neoadjuvant response prediction 160
- Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with 161 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of cases 33,34 . The 162 predominant subtypes of NSCLC are lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous 163 cell carcinoma (LUSC) 35 . The choice of treatment for NSCLC is multifaceted, tailored 164 according to the stage of the disease, histopathological findings, genetic aberrations, and 165 the overall health of patients 36 . A comprehensive treatment strategy typically includes 166 surgery,  radiation  therapy,  chemotherapy,  immunotherapy,  and  molecularly  targeted 167 treatments 37 . For patients with localized NSCLC, early surgical intervention is available, 168 yet  the  five-year  survival  rate  stands  at  a  mere  59%.  Prognostically  valuable  features 169 extracted  from  lung  CT  scans  are  critically  important  for  developing  precise,  non170 invasive imaging-based NSCLC treatment protocols. 171

Consequently, we evaluated the efficacy of LCTfound on the prognostic imaging

of NSCLC on the LUNG1 dataset (420 scans). We dedicated approximately half of the

22

LUNG1 dataset

(220 scans) to fine-tune the model, and the other half (200 scans), which remained  unseen  during  training,  was  utilized  for  testing  the  model.  The  model

incorporates both Lung CT images and tumor localization information as simultaneous inputs  to  improve  prognostic  accuracy.  We  conducted  a  comparative  analysis  of

LCTfound, Foundation

22

,  Med3D

38

,  and  MG

39

investigate  the  performance  disparities

between models that were fully fine-tuned and those that only had their terminal linear

- classifier  fine-tuned  maintaining  the  feature  extraction  part  frozen  (Fig  2a-h).  In  the 180

LUNG1 cohort, the strategy of fine-tuning the full LCTfound model surpassed the other 181 seven baseline performances, achieving an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.704 (95% 182 CI  0.626-0.777)  (Supplementary  Fig.  4),  surpassed  the  runner-up  by  14.7%  (AUC  is 183 0.6134).. For LCTfound, all results yielded statistically significant results, regardless of 184 whether we entailed full model fine-tuning or mere adjustments to the linear classifier(P 185 <0.05). Beyond AUC, the Kaplan-Meier survival estimates indicated that the fine-tuned 186 LCTfound model provided superior stratification (P < 0.001), confirming its efficacy in 187 accurately identifying mortality-based risk groups. By integrating the Grad-CAM, we 188 generated saliency maps for LCTfound in the process of NSCLC prognosis prediction, 189 revealing  the  attention  of  model  focus  on  diseased  regions  which  underscores  its 190 sensitivity to clinical problems (Supplementary Fig. 5). We also introduce perturbations 191 to the input images to demonstrate the stability of LCTfound(Supplementary Fig. 6). 192

Meanwhile, we validated the proficiency of LCTfound in few-shot learning to 193 prognosticate the major pathological response(MPR) elicited by neoadjuvant 194 chemoimmunotherapy  in  lung  cancer 40-43 .  We  gathered  a  data  cohort  from  four 195 centers(the first affiliated hospital of Guangzhou Medical University , Liaoning Cancer 196 Hospital & Institute , Shanghai chest hospital , and the first affiliated hospital of Xi'an 197 Jiaotong University), composed of lung CT scans and the associated outcomes of MPR 198 after  treatment..  We  fine-tuned  three  pre-trained  models  (LCTfound,  MAE 29 ,  and 199 RadImageNet 44 )  using 876 images from 90 lung CT scans; the internal testing dataset 200 included 74 images from 74 lung CT scans; the external testing dataset contained 82 201 images from 82 lung CT scans(Supplementary Fig. 7). LCTfound attained the highest 202 AUROC on  both  the  internal  and  external  test  sets,  whether  using  lung  window  or 203 mediastinal window CT images(Fig 2i-p). In addition, we compared the best parameters 204 from the training phase and the terminal parameters obtained at the end of the training 205 phase for all three models, and LCTfound exceeded the other two models(Supplementary 206 Fig. 8). 207

# LCTfound facilitates the diagnosis of uncommon lung diseases
The  construction  of  AI  models  targeting  uncommon  lung  diseases  frequently 209 encounters  challenges  stemming  from  the  limited  availability  of  the  training  data. 210 Mediastinal neoplasms are classic low-incidence thoracic diseases with a variety of types, 211 ranging  from  benign  to  malignant  growth 45 .  The  global  incidence  of  mediastinal 212 neoplasms is approximately 0.77-1.68%, with about 60 million to 130 million patients 213 worldwide 46 . The preceding decade has witnessed a steady increase in the incidence of 214 mediastinal  neoplasms,  associated  with  a  poor  prognosis  for  patients  with  malignant 215 forms. Currently, CT-based  diagnosis  of mediastinal neoplasms  is fraught with 216 substantial  practical  difficulties.  The  structural  similarities  and  close  proximity  of 217 mediastinal  neoplasms  to  normal  mediastinal  anatomy  frequently  result  in  diagnostic 218 ambiguity,  thus  complicating  the  comprehensive  detection  and  precise  localization  of 219 mediastinal neoplasms in regular CT imaging (Fig 3a). 220

By focusing on the diagnosis of Mediastinal neoplasms, we demonstrated the few221 shot learning ability of LCTFound, which is instrumental in the diagnosis of such low222 incidence diseases. We standardized data collection from seven medical centers by the 223 same  protocol  and  collaborated  with  seasoned  physicians  for  meticulous  pixel-level 224 tumor annotations. From these centers, the dataset included: 258 scans from The First 225 Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University (96 designated for training, 84 for 226 validation, and 78 for testing) and four external medical centers provided 232 lung CT 227 scans in total for testing. (Supplementary Data Table 1). The compendium comprises 590 228 lung  CT  scans,  with  the  patient  cohort  ranging  in  age  from  1  to  84  years,  and  the 229 assemblage of data extending from 2009 to 2020. It includes a delineation of 192 benign 230 and  408  malignant  cases(Supplementary  Fig.  9).  Rigorous  de-identification  protocols 231 were  employed  on  all  images  within  the  database,  thereby  upholding  the  sanctity  of 232 patient privacy. 233

We compared the LCTFound pre-trained on LungCT-28M with publicly accessible 234 pre-trained  models  for  lung  CT:  MedSAM 30 ,  MAE 29 , InternImage 47 ,  Swin3D 48 , 235 Universal 49 .  Additionally,  we  incorporated  a  U-net  model  that  had  been  trained 236 specifically on our assembled and annotated dataset of mediastinal neoplasms. The results 237 from our investigation conclusively indicates that LCTFound surpasses its 238 counterparts(Fig 3b). Within the internal datasets, LCTFound achieved the Dice score 239 apex of 0.7895, surpassing the subsequent leading model (MedSAM) by a margin of 240 5.08%. This trend of superiority was consistent across five external datasets: In external 241 test  set  1,  LCTFound  exceeds  the  runner-up  MAE  by  0.25%;  in  external  test  set  2, 242 LCTFound surpasses the second-best MAE by 1.58%; in external test set 3, LCTFound 243 outperforms the second-place Universal by 2.30%; in external test set 4, LCTFound is 244 above the second-place MAE by 7.90%; in external test set 5, LCTFound outpaces the 245 second-place MAE by 3.64%(Fig 3a). Overall, LCTFound has demonstrated unparalleled 246 effectiveness in the segmentation of low-incidence mediastinal neoplasms , showcasing 247 its adeptness in few-shot learning(Supplementary Video 1). We visualized the saliency 248 map of LCTfound using lung CT images with mediastinal neoplasms to highlight the 249 significance of individual pixels in the segmentation process. The alignment between the 250 visualization of saliency maps and clinical features underlines the efficacy of LCTfound 251 in extracting clinically relevant information (Supplementary Fig. 10). 252

Furthermore, we verified the effectiveness of the pre-trained LCTfound in diagnosing

pulmonary  alveolar  proteinosis  (PAP)

50,51

,  leveraging  a  small  dataset  for  fine-tuning.

PAP, a rare  lung  disease,  is  a  syndrome  characterized  by  surfactant  accumulation  on alveoli and impaired alveolar macrophages, leading to insidious progressive respiratory

difficulty,  hypoxic  respiratory  failure,  secondary  infections,  and  pulmonary  fibrosis

52

.

Prevalence rates range from 3.7 to 40 cases per million (depending on the country/region)

with  an  incidence  estimated  at  0.2  cases  per  million

53

.  We  compiled  a  dataset  from

- Guangzhou First People's Hospital, comprising 270 cases of PAP-positive CT scan results 260

(Supplementary Fig. 11). The training dataset we developed includes 27 cases of PAP261 positive CT scans (4,835 images) and 270 individual scans (58,008 images) may contain 262 health and other diseases, while the test dataset contains 243 PAP-positive cases (37,756 263 images) and 2430 scans from non-PAP individuals (541,038 images). On the test dataset, 264 we assessed the performance of LCTfound, MAE 29 , and RadImageNet, all of which were 265 fully pre-trained on the LungCT-28Mdataset and subsequently fine-tuned on the training 266 dataset. LCTfound achieved an area under ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.9532, surpassing 267 the second-place MAE by 6.01%. We halved the training dataset (13 PAP-positive cases 268 with 2,191 images, 135 negative cases with 29,992 images) and fine-tuned the three pre269 trained models. LCTfound maintained the lead with an AUROC of 0.9130, outperforming 270 the  second-place  MAE  by  5.54%.  This  demonstrates  the  efficacy  of  the  pre-trained 271 LCTfound in diagnosing rare lung diseases through few-shot learning(Supplementary 272 Fig.  12).  The  saliency  map  of  the  PAP  image  reveals  that  the  fine-tuned  LCTfound 273 successfully  extracted  the  clinical  features  of  PAP,  such  as  the  accumulation  of 274 anomalous substances in the alveoli(Supplementary Fig. 13). 275

# Discussion 398
In this study, we collated a large multicenter dataset of over 100 million lung CT 399 images from 485,885 lung CT scans, and by combining diagnostic reports and image 400 quality,  we  established  the  LungCT-28M pre-training dataset which includes 105,184 401 lung CT scans (over 20 million images) covering the common 14 lung diseases as well 402 as  healthy  lungs.  Using  a  self-supervised  training  strategy,  we  developed  a  new 403 foundation model for lung CT, LCTfound, and valided this model with multiple high404 level  and  low-level  clinical  tasks.  We  demonstrated  the  following  outcomes.  First,  to 405 assess the efficacy of LCTfound in diagnosing uncommon lung diseases, we showed that 406 LCTfound outperformed other pre-training models, achieving the highest accuracy in 407 both localizing mediastinal neoplasms and diagnosing PAP. The diagnosis of uncommon 408 diseases is clinically significant, and these experiments highlight LCTfound's potential 409 for generalization in tasks related to diagnosing such conditions. Second, we showed that 410 LCTfound improves neoadjuvant reponse and NSCLS prognostication prediction. Theses 411 tasks holds significant clinical value and LCTfound advanced the progress in this field, 412 although  it  is  still  some  distance  away  from  clinical  implementation.  Third,  as  an 413 important  technique  for  surgical  navigation,  we  showed  that  LCTfound  has  superior 414 performance for whole lung segmentation. Fourth, LCTfound demonstrated significant 415 improvements in lung CT imaging tasks, including virtual lung CTA imaging, optimizing 416 reconstructions from sparse-view CT scans, and denoising low-dose lung CT images to 417 enhance overall image quality. These various tasks that LCTfound could perform are 418

- useful in many clinical settings and disease conditions. 419

We compared LCTfound with other models. Compared with other vision-centric 420 encoders,  We  showed  that  LCTfound  pre-trained  with  the  DDPM  strategy  could  be 421 employed for a wider variety of clinical tasks related to lung CT. LCTfound was more 422 adept at pixel-level tasks like CT images denoising and reconstruction than pre-trained 423 models such as MAE 29 and MedSAM 30 , enabling ordinary lung CT imaging machines to 424 attain superior imaging capabilities. LCTfound goes beyond the capabilities of GANs by 425 infusing pixel-level tasks with richer image details, effectively enhancing lung CT images 426 regardless  of  their  initial  quality.  Its  DDPM-driven  training  enables  it  to  extract  key 427 semantic elements, capable of delineating the lung anatomy even from images plagued 428 with substantial noise. This ensures that in high-level semantic tasks such as lung disease 429 diagnosis or localization, LCTfound also achieved superior results. Especially in the task 430 of full lung segmentation, whether it is for anatomical structures with many details such 431 as  Trachea,  Vein,  and  artery,  or  for  other  mass  structures,  LCTfound  demonstrates 432 consistent performance. Furthermore, the special strategy of DDPM has expanded the 433 diversity of the model. With the input of different time steps, different time embeddings 434 endow LCTfound with the ability to extract features at various levels. We are convinced 435 that  LCTfound  will  revolutionize  the  foundational  vision-based  models  for  lung  CT 436 images and advance the progress of large models in medicine. 437

As  a  foundational  model,  pre-trained  on  over  28  million  lung  CT  images, 438 LCTfound can perform a wide array of clinical applications, particularly in scenarios with 439 limited  data  availability.  In  developing  data-driven  AI  approaches,  acquiring  actual 440 clinical data typically involves addressing the issue of patient privacy 69 ; otherwise, the 441 data cannot be exported from the hospital. With LCTfound, it is possible to simulate and 442 generate a multitude of synthetic lung CT images with varying window widths and levels, 443 aiding AI model training and validation. Designing various adapters based on LCTfound 444 enables fine-tuning of the model with multicenter hospital data, which allows the data to 445 remain within the hospital, but the model to be shared among multiple medical centers, 446

achieving effective federated learning. LCTfound is a model pre-trained based on the 447 DDPM  strategy,  thus  it  possesses  inherent  advantages  in  low-level  tasks,  such  as 448 converting  lung  CT  images  into  CT  pulmonary  angiography  images.  CT  pulmonary 449 angiography 70 ,  which  images  the  pulmonary  arteries,  is  a  crucial  tool  for  diagnosing 450 pulmonary embolism, but it requires the traumatic insertion of an intravenous catheter 451 into the patient 71 . Developing a reliable method for virtually transforming from ordinary 452 lung CT scans to CT pulmonary angiography images would be beneficial in alleviating 453 patient discomfort and advancing large-scale disease screening. From the perspective of 454 data compression, we posit that the adequately pre-trained LCTfound embodies extensive 455 information from numerous lung CT images, facilitating the substantial compression of 456 large datasets that are previously cumbersome to duplicate and disseminate. In essence, 457 LCTfound encapsulates a vast repository of lung CT scans into a fundamental model, 458 ready to tackle diverse tasks in lung CT imaging and position itself as the intelligent brain 459 of lung CT imaging. 460

Our study had several limitations. For example, for practical clinical applications, 461 the  operational  speed  of  the  model  is  crucial  for  doctors,  particularly  in  the  case  of 462 intraoperative lung CT imaging, which may demand the real-time processing of captured 463 data. The contradiction to the demand for real-time processing is the limited computing 464 resources  of  hospitals,  hence,  undertaking  a  series  of  AI  acceleration  techniques  like 465 pruning 72 , distillation 73 , and quantization 74 on LCTfound is the forthcoming task. # Network architecture of LCTfound. 484
- The  main  architecture  of  LCTfound  is  a  CrossAttention-based  U-shape  network 485 (Supplementary Fig. 1). 486

LCTfound employs an innovative image self-supervised approach, specifically utilizing 487 diffusion  models  for  pre-training  to  obtain  robust  feature  representations.  Diffusion 488 models are capable of generating realistic and diverse images, and numerous studies have 489 demonstrated that well-trained diffusion models contain rich prior knowledge, which can 490 significantly aid in small sample tasks 79 . To better acquire feature representations across 491 multiple levels, we opted for a pixel-to-pixel space diffusion model rather than the Latent 492 Diffusion  Model  (LDM).  The  diffusion  training  process  in  LDM  occurs  in  the  latent 493 space, which can hinder the learning of robust low-level visual features. For LCTfound, 494 we  designed  a  UNet  model  architecture  enhanced  with  a  cross-attention  mechanism, 495 enabling  the  model  to  generate  images  with  supplementary  textual  information. 496 Specifically, LCTfound features five downsampling modules, five upsampling modules, 497 and one deep feature extraction module. Each of these modules incorporates residual 498 structures  to  ensure  effective  gradient  optimization  during  training. Moreover, certain 499 downsampling and upsampling modules are enhanced with a cross-attention Transformer 500 module,  further  improving  the  model's  ability  to  capture  detailed  and  contextually 501 relevant features. This mechanism enables the encoded textual information to directly 502 influence  the  image  generation  process.  Such  textual  information  includes,  but  is  not 503 limited to, parameters like the image's window width and window level, as well as disease 504 category  information  extracted  from  reports  using  NLP  models.  In  visual  tasks, 505 convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have good efficiency, speed, and generalization 506 capabilities.  However, owing to their inherent inductive biases, they often struggle to 507 effectively  capture  global  contextual  information.  Incorporating  Transformer-based 508 attention modules addresses this limitation by enabling the model to achieve superior 509

- global feature capture 80 . This hybrid architecture leverages the strengths of both CNNs 510 and  Transformers,  resulting  in  a  more  robust  model.  Additionally,  the  upsampling, 511 downsampling, and deep feature extraction modules not only accept image features as 512 inputs but also receive encoded time step information. This integration allows the model 513 to  better  estimate  the  noise  present  at  each  point  in  the  diffusion  process,  thereby 514 improving the  overall  accuracy  and  reliability  of  the  extracted  feature  maps.  A  more 515 detailed  description  of  the  structural  information,  including  the  specific  designs  and 516 implementation details, will be provided in the supplementary methods section. 517

# Abstract
The concomitant development and evolution of lung computed tomography (CT) and 26 artificial intelligence (AI) has allowed non-invasive lung imaging to be a key part of the 27 clinical care of patients with major diseases, such as lung cancer. However, the paucity 28 of labeled lung CT data has limited the training highly efficacious AI models and thereby 29 has retarded broad-scale adoption and deployment of AI-based lung CT imaging in the 30 real-world clinical setting. In this paper, We introduce LCTfound, a foundational model 31 that encodes images along with correlated clinical information, into a neural network. 32 LCTfound used self-supervised learning pre-trained by diffusion models using a large 33 dataset containing 105,184 lung CT scans (totaling more than 28 million images) from 34 multiple centers. LCTfound was evaluated on 8 categories of lung CT tasks, ranging from 35 scanning-level clinical diagnosis to pixel-level image restoration, including segmentation 36 of mediastinal neoplasm, diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, prognosis of non37 small  cell  lung  cancer,  prediction  of  major  pathological  response  to  neoadjuvant 38 chemoimmunotherapy,  whole  lung  3D  modeling  for  surgical  navigation,  virtual  lung 39 computed tomography angiography(CTA), reconstruction of lung CT from sparse views, 40 and enhancement of low-dose CT images. Equipped with the robust few-shot learning 41 capability, LCTfound outperformed the previously state-of-the-art pre-trained models in 42 all the above tasks. LCTfound is a major advancements in self-supervised representation 43 learning on lung CT, laying the groundwork for a foundational model that operates with 44 high efficacy across the spectrum of low-level and high-level clinical tasks and serving a 45 dual purpose in aiding in clinical diagnosis of lung diseases and improving the quality of 46 lung CT imaging. 47

48

# Introduction 49
- As an integral part of clinical imaging, the lung computed tomography (CT) is crucial for 50 doctors to examine the structure and function of key anatomical regions within the chest, 51 including the heart, lungs, related system organs including blood vessels and the spine 152 5 .  Annually,  hundreds  of  millions  of  lung  CT  are  performed  globally  as  lung  CT  is 53 indispensable  for  a  multitude  of  clinical  tasks,  ranging  from  disease  detection 6 and 54 continuous monitoring of disease states, to diagnostic evaluation of common and rare 55 lung  condition  to  preoperative  strategic  planning.  Concurrently,  the  development, 56 evolution and application of medical AI systems for lung CT has substantially eased the 57 workload in areas such as surgical navigation for lung operations, staging of lung cancer 7 , 58 and prognosis for lung cancer 8,9 , while also augmenting the imaging capabilities of lung 59
- CT systems. 60
- However, the creation of newer and more sophisticated medical AI systems typically 61 relies on massive amounts and meticulously curated datasets that require laborious and 62 time-intensive labeling that are tailored for specific clinical downstream tasks. The lack 63 of doctors with domain knowledge in lung CT and the prolonged process of gathering 64 sufficient data render the compilation of large, annotated datasets for individual lung CT 65 scans and related medical tasks costly and challenging 10-12 . This is particularly true for 66 rare  lung  diseases,  where  obtaining  enough  clinical  cases  to  train  comprehensive  AI 67 models is often impractical, leading to limitations in the performance of the currently 68 trained AI lung CT models. 69
- With  a  breakthroughs  in  large  language  and  vision  models  like  ChatGPT 13-15 , 70 CLIP 16 ,  SimCLR 17 ,  and DINO 18 ,  medical foundation models are now providing novel 71 solutions  to  address  theses  chanllenges.  Foundation  models  have  been  developed  in 72 computational pathology 1 , ophthalmic disease diagnosis 20,21 , ultrasonography, and cancer 73 biomarker innovation 22 , improving diagnostic accuracy, facilitating knowledge sharing 23 , 74

and  furthering  medical  education.  Foundational  models  that  are  trained  via  self75 supervised  learning  (SSL)  on  extremely  large  datasets  without  labelling.  Foundation 76 models are proficient at learning knowledge representations with ability for zero-shot or 77 few-shot learning, enabling these models to be fine-tuned for a multitude of downstream 78 applications 24 . 79

Foundation models for lung CT have not yet been developed, despite the board 80 applications of AI in the field of lung CT. For example, AI integrates the outcomes of 81 lung CT examination with clinical symptoms, exposure history, and laboratory tests to 82 quickly diagnose COVID-19 in patients 8,25,26 .  Three-dimensional deep learning neural 83 networks,  leveraging  low-dose  lung  CT  imaging,  enable  lung  cancer  screening,  with 84 diagnostic accuracy that exceeds radiologists 7 . A modularized neural network has been 85 engineered for reconstructing low-dose lung CT images, achieving a reconstruction speed 86 that greatly outpaces commercialized iterative approaches, while maintaining the quality 87 of the reconstruction 27 . Thus, foundation models in lung CT imaging can be expected to 88 serve  a  dual  purpose:  offering  clinical  insights  to  provide  diagnostic  and  therapeutic 89 support  and  enhancing  the  imaging  technology  of  CT  scanners  to  improve  practical 90 operations. 91

In  this  study,  we  present  LCTfound,  a  lung  CT  foundational  model  integrating 92 images with correlated fundamental clinical infomation into the neural network, which is 93 pre-trained by the diffusion policy on LungCT-28M (Fig. 1a) to address the dual purpose 94 role of lung CT. We used the LungCT-28M dataset is an extensive collection tailored for 95 lung CT, incorporating 105,184 lung CT scans from 5 centers, comprising over 28 million 96 images that encompass 14 distinct diseases(Fig. 1b). To our knowledge, this represents 97 the largest lung CT dataset to date, covering the widest range of comprehensive disease 98 states. By capitalizing on the LungCT-28M, we developed a feature encoder and decoder 99 employing SSL through a denoising diffusion probabilistic model 28 (DDPM, Fig. 1c), 100

which is adept at few-shot generalization across multiple downstream tasks leveraging 101 the extracted features. We validated the clinical and technical significance of LCTfound 102 across scaning-level to pixel-level downstream tasks. These tasks include the diagnosis 103 of low-incidence diseases (e.g., mediastinal neoplasm and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis 104 (PAP)), the prognosis prediction of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLS), the prediction 105 of major pathological response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, three-dimensional 106 whole lung modelingvirtual lung CTA imaging, the reconstruction of sparse views lung 107 CT and the enhancement of low dose lung CT (Fig. 1d). When benchmarked against 108 conventional vision pre-trained models such as like MAE 29 and MedSAM 30 in these tasks, 109 LCTfound  consistently outperformed these counterparts (with an average  7.5% 110 improvement  over  the  second-ranked  models,  and  a  maximum  20%  increase  in 111 performance over existing models). 112
# Results 113

# Curation of LungCT-28M and rationale of LCTfound 114
We  assembled  a  large  national  lung  CT  dataset,  with  485,885  scans,  from  patients 115 enrolled between 2009 and 2023 over 15 years (276,755 males and 209,130 females,) 116 from five medical centers across China (Fig. 1a). We refined this dataset based on the 117 quality  of  images  and  the  completeness  of  diagnostic  information  provided  in  the 118 accompanying medical reports. This process culminated in the creation of the pre-training 119 dataset,  LungCT-28M (Fig. 1a, Methods), which encompasses 105,184 scans (59,935 120 from males and 45,249 from females). Excluding the cohort of 14,756 Lung CT scans 121 with  no  evidence  of  disease,  the  final  LungCT-28M  dataset  for  training  the  model 122 comprised  CT  scans  for  14  common  lung  diseases,  with  the  following  distribution: 123 Diffuse parenchymal lung diseases (DPLD, 49,133 scans), pulmonary calcification (PC, 124 36,379 scans), Pulmonary bullae (PB, 19,029 scans), Lymph node enlargement (LNE, 125 16,967  scans),  Pulmonary  fibrosis  (PF,  16,945  scans),  bronchiectasis  (BCH,  16,302 126 scans),  Emphysema  (13,961  scans),  Pleural  effusion  (PE,  12,326  scans),  Pulmonary 127

cavity (PC, 5,544 scans), atelectasis (5,169 scans), Pneumothorax (PTX, 2,798 scans), 128 Tracheal  mass  (TM,  1,535  scans),  Mediastinal  mass  (MM,  1,444  scans),  and  Rib 129 Fractures (RF, 649 scans) (Fig. 1b). The primary scanning protocol of LungCT-28M is 130 chiefly  guided by clinical application requirements, specifically choosing the window 131 width and window level. 132

During  the  training  phase,  we  employed  a  U-net  architecture  enhanced  by  the 133 integration of transformer blocks 31 , encompassing roughly 200M trainable 134 parameters(Supplementary Fig. 1). Paired clinical information (such as window width, 135 window level,  etc.)  was  randomly  selected  and  after  Bert  encoding,  coupled  with  its 136 corresponding lung CT images, inputed into the main backbone network of LCTfound. 137 The  self-supervised  pre-training  LCTfound  is  grounded  in  the  core  principles  of 138 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM): A two-dimensional lung CT image 139 and its  basic  information  were  randomly  selected  from  the  LungCT-28M  dataset  and 140 subjected to data augmentation. During the forward propagation, we progressively added 141 Gaussian noise with a specific intensity into the image. After 1000 steps, this process 142 resulted in the transformation of the image into pure noise (Fig. 1c). During the backward 143 propagation, the neural network  learnt to perform denoising, thereby acquiring 144 representation learning abilities(Methods). The basic information of the lung CT images 145 was  used  as  guidance,  being  input  into  the  model  simultaneously.  To  strengthen  the 146 robustness  of  the  main  backbone  network  to  these  basic  information,  we  randomly 147 occluded part or all of the basic information as input. For the inference stage, the pre148 trained LCTfound was employed as a potent image encoder-decoder. For localization of 149 mediastinal neoplasms and whole lung segmentation, we applyed a trainable multilayer 150 perceptron  (MLP)  during  fine-tuning  process.  This  MLP  served  as  a  fusion  layer  for 151 features  integrating  from  the  decoding  path  to  obtain  the  final  segmentation  mask 152 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). For tasks like PAP diagnosis and NSCLC prognosis prediction, 153 we employ a trainable MLP to transform the bottom output features of the encoder to 154

- diagnostic labels(Supplementary Fig. 2b). For pixel-level tasks such as sparse-view lung 155 CT reconstruction, LCTfound was used as a feature dictionary to guide the restoration of 156 low-quality lung CT images(Supplementary Fig. 3a). For low-dose lung CT 157 enhancement, LCTfound was fine-tuned on downsteam task data through cold-diffusion 158 manner 32 (Supplementary Fig. 3b). 159

# LCTfound improves NSCLC prognostication and neoadjuvant response prediction 160
- Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with 161 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of cases 33,34 . The 162 predominant subtypes of NSCLC are lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous 163 cell carcinoma (LUSC) 35 . # Discussion 398
In this study, we collated a large multicenter dataset of over 100 million lung CT 399 images from 485,885 lung CT scans, and by combining diagnostic reports and image 400 quality,  we  established  the  LungCT-28M pre-training dataset which includes 105,184 401 lung CT scans (over 20 million images) covering the common 14 lung diseases as well 402 as  healthy  lungs.  Using  a  self-supervised  training  strategy,  we  developed  a  new 403 foundation model for lung CT, LCTfound, and valided this model with multiple high404 level  and  low-level  clinical  tasks.  We  demonstrated  the  following  outcomes.  First,  to 405 assess the efficacy of LCTfound in diagnosing uncommon lung diseases, we showed that 406 LCTfound outperformed other pre-training models, achieving the highest accuracy in 407 both localizing mediastinal neoplasms and diagnosing PAP. The diagnosis of uncommon 408 diseases is clinically significant, and these experiments highlight LCTfound's potential 409 for generalization in tasks related to diagnosing such conditions. Second, we showed that 410 LCTfound improves neoadjuvant reponse and NSCLS prognostication prediction. Theses 411 tasks holds significant clinical value and LCTfound advanced the progress in this field, 412 although  it  is  still  some  distance  away  from  clinical  implementation.  Third,  as  an 413 important  technique  for  surgical  navigation,  we  showed  that  LCTfound  has  superior 414 performance for whole lung segmentation. Fourth, LCTfound demonstrated significant 415 improvements in lung CT imaging tasks, including virtual lung CTA imaging, optimizing 416 reconstructions from sparse-view CT scans, and denoising low-dose lung CT images to 417 enhance overall image quality. These various tasks that LCTfound could perform are 418

- useful in many clinical settings and disease conditions. 419

We compared LCTfound with other models. Compared with other vision-centric 420 encoders,  We  showed  that  LCTfound  pre-trained  with  the  DDPM  strategy  could  be 421 employed for a wider variety of clinical tasks related to lung CT. LCTfound was more 422 adept at pixel-level tasks like CT images denoising and reconstruction than pre-trained 423 models such as MAE 29 and MedSAM 30 , enabling ordinary lung CT imaging machines to 424 attain superior imaging capabilities. LCTfound goes beyond the capabilities of GANs by 425 infusing pixel-level tasks with richer image details, effectively enhancing lung CT images 426 regardless  of  their  initial  quality.  Its  DDPM-driven  training  enables  it  to  extract  key 427 semantic elements, capable of delineating the lung anatomy even from images plagued 428 with substantial noise. Especially in the task 430 of full lung segmentation, whether it is for anatomical structures with many details such 431 as  Trachea,  Vein,  and  artery,  or  for  other  mass  structures,  LCTfound  demonstrates 432 consistent performance. Furthermore, the special strategy of DDPM has expanded the 433 diversity of the model. With the input of different time steps, different time embeddings 434 endow LCTfound with the ability to extract features at various levels. We are convinced 435 that  LCTfound  will  revolutionize  the  foundational  vision-based  models  for  lung  CT 436 images and advance the progress of large models in medicine. 437

As  a  foundational  model,  pre-trained  on  over  28  million  lung  CT  images, 438 LCTfound can perform a wide array of clinical applications, particularly in scenarios with 439 limited  data  availability.  In  developing  data-driven  AI  approaches,  acquiring  actual 440 clinical data typically involves addressing the issue of patient privacy 69 ; otherwise, the 441 data cannot be exported from the hospital. # Network architecture of LCTfound. 484
- The  main  architecture  of  LCTfound  is  a  CrossAttention-based  U-shape  network 485 (Supplementary Fig. 1). 486

LCTfound employs an innovative image self-supervised approach, specifically utilizing 487 diffusion  models  for  pre-training  to  obtain  robust  feature  representations.  Diffusion 488 models are capable of generating realistic and diverse images, and numerous studies have 489 demonstrated that well-trained diffusion models contain rich prior knowledge, which can 490 significantly aid in small sample tasks 79 . To better acquire feature representations across 491 multiple levels, we opted for a pixel-to-pixel space diffusion model rather than the Latent 492 Diffusion  Model  (LDM).  The  diffusion  training  process  in  LDM  occurs  in  the  latent 493 space, which can hinder the learning of robust low-level visual features. For LCTfound, 494 we  designed  a  UNet  model  architecture  enhanced  with  a  cross-attention  mechanism, 495 enabling  the  model  to  generate  images  with  supplementary  textual  information. 496 Specifically, LCTfound features five downsampling modules, five upsampling modules, 497 and one deep feature extraction module. Each of these modules incorporates residual 498 structures  to  ensure  effective  gradient  optimization  during  training. Moreover, certain 499 downsampling and upsampling modules are enhanced with a cross-attention Transformer 500 module,  further  improving  the  model's  ability  to  capture  detailed  and  contextually 501 relevant features. This mechanism enables the encoded textual information to directly 502 influence  the  image  generation  process.  Such  textual  information  includes,  but  is  not 503 limited to, parameters like the image's window width and window level, as well as disease 504 category  information  extracted  from  reports  using  NLP  models.  In  visual  tasks, 505 convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have good efficiency, speed, and generalization 506 capabilities.  However, owing to their inherent inductive biases, they often struggle to 507 effectively  capture  global  contextual  information.  Incorporating  Transformer-based 508 attention modules addresses this limitation by enabling the model to achieve superior 509

- global feature capture 80 . This hybrid architecture leverages the strengths of both CNNs 510 and  Transformers,  resulting  in  a  more  robust  model.  Additionally,  the  upsampling, 511 downsampling, and deep feature extraction modules not only accept image features as 512 inputs but also receive encoded time step information. This integration allows the model 513 to  better  estimate  the  noise  present  at  each  point  in  the  diffusion  process,  thereby 514 improving the  overall  accuracy  and  reliability  of  the  extracted  feature  maps.
